title: History 13: Seeing in 3D: NeRF, Gaussian splats and structured latents

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the primary computational trade-off between Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting?
options: NeRF is faster to render but lower fidelity; Gaussian Splatting is slower but higher fidelity.
NeRF offers continuous, high-fidelity representations but is slow to render; Gaussian Splatting offers explicit, real-time rendering but requires managing explicit primitives.
NeRF requires more VRAM than Gaussian Splatting in all cases.
Gaussian Splatting is an implicit representation while NeRF is an explicit representation.
questions.answer: NeRF offers continuous, high-fidelity representations but is slow to render; Gaussian Splatting offers explicit, real-time rendering but requires managing explicit primitives.
questions.why: The 'Why this matters' section explicitly states: 'NeRFs offer continuous, high-fidelity representations but are slow to render; Gaussian Splatting offers explicit, real-time rendering but requires careful management of explicit primitives.'

questions.q: In the context of the `TripoSplat` module, what type of 3D representation does the final output constitute, and why?
options: Implicit, because it uses a transformer to generate the scene.
Implicit, because the diffusion process in latent space is implicit.
Explicit, because the decoder outputs explicit Gaussian parameters such as position, scale, and rotation.
Explicit, because it uses a 5D coordinate function.
questions.answer: Explicit, because the decoder outputs explicit Gaussian parameters such as position, scale, and rotation.
questions.why: The 'Common mistakes' section clarifies: 'In TripoSplat, the transformer generates explicit Gaussian parameters... the final 3D representation is explicit.' The 'Under the hood' section lists these parameters as position, scale, rotation, color, and opacity.

questions.q: Based on the lab results provided in the lesson, what is the calculated transmittance ($T$) for the third slice ($T_3$) when the opacity ($\alpha$) of the previous slices is 0.5?
questions.why: The 'Lab' section shows the output line `RESULT transmittance = 1 0.5 0.25` and explains the calculation: '$T_3 = T_2 (1 - \alpha_2) = 0.5 \times (1 - 0.5) = 0.25$'.

questions.q: What specific method in the `comfy/ldm/chroma_radiance` module is designed to prevent VRAM exhaustion on large scenes, and how does it achieve this?
options: The `forward_nerf` method, by using a 5D coordinate function.
The `render_splat` function, by projecting Gaussians to 2D screen space.
The `forward_tiled_nerf` method, by processing inputs in chunks.
The `GaussianModel` class, by storing anisotropic covariance.
questions.answer: The `forward_tiled_nerf` method, by processing inputs in chunks.
questions.why: The 'In ComfyUI' section states: 'The `forward_tiled_nerf` offers a memory-optimized version by processing inputs in chunks.' The 'Common mistakes' section adds: 'Using `forward_nerf` without `forward_tiled_nerf` on large scenes can exhaust VRAM.'

questions.q: In the volume rendering equation for NeRF, what does the term $T_i$ (transmittance) represent, and how is it defined recursively?
questions.answer: It represents the probability that light reaches slice $i$ without being absorbed by previous slices. It is defined recursively as $T_1 = 1$ and $T_i = T_{i-1} (1 - \alpha_{i-1})$.
questions.why: The 'Under the hood' section defines $T_i$ as 'the probability that light reaches slice $i$ without being absorbed by previous slices' and provides the recursive formulas: '$T_1 = 1$' and '$T_i = T_{i-1} (1 - \alpha_{i-1})$'.
